column3: The hardest challenge is separating the real causes from visible symptoms while coordinating DPE support with franchisee accountability. A store can underperform because of local demand, unit economics, operational execution, capability or several factors at once. DPE would need timely shared evidence, a named case owner and clear escalation rights, while still respecting franchisee autonomy and acting before the situation deteriorates further.
column4: Based on the public context, I would expect: (1) a sustained performance trigger and formal case owner; (2) a joint fact-finding review with the franchisee to validate financial, customer and operational data; (3) root-cause diagnosis covering local market, unit economics, people/capability, service execution and compliance; (4) a root-cause-linked recovery plan with owners, DPE support, milestones, measurable outcomes and escalation rules; (5) regular monitoring plus formal review gates; and (6) a governed decision to continue, revise or close recovery, or consider transfer, refranchising or closure if recovery is not viable. This is professional judgement, not a claim about DPE?€?s internal procedure.
column5: Three areas: (1) store unit economics and trend?€?sales/transactions, food and labour costs, delivery costs, margins and cash constraints; (2) operational execution and capability?€?staffing/rosters, training, product quality, availability, service/delivery times, complaints and customer measures; and (3) local market and governance?€?catchment demand, competition, pricing/promotions, franchisee engagement, compliance and ability to fund or lead the recovery.

column7: Executing the agreed recovery actions and mobilising support
column8: I would investigate execution first because that is where a sound diagnosis and plan must become coordinated action. Missing owners, insufficient support, delayed tasks or inconsistent store adoption can make a valid plan appear ineffective. Checking implementation fidelity and resource mobilisation helps distinguish a bad diagnosis from a good plan that was not actually carried out.
column9: Reassess the evidence and causes before deciding the next action
column15: The explanation is convincing because inconsistency breaks the chain between evidence, action, ownership and review. Different diagnoses or review rules can create delay, rework and unclear accountability. I rated it 4 rather than 5 because organisational inconsistency is not the only cause: weak local demand, unsustainable unit economics, external shocks or franchisee capability may remain decisive even with a well-controlled intervention process.
column16: Intervention process & control ?€? diagnosis, recovery planning, execution and follow-up
column17: I would prioritise intervention process and control because it connects detection to a decision and then to measurable action. A common stage-gated process can reduce variation, make handoffs visible and show whether recovery is working. Governance and decision rights are a close second, because the named case owner must also have authority to obtain support and escalate.
column18: Introduce one stage-gated Franchise Recovery Case Playbook with a named case owner. Each case would use a common diagnostic data pack, a root-cause-linked action plan, named owners and support, a weekly action/evidence log, formal review gates and predetermined escalation rights. This would reduce avoidable variation and rework, speed decisions and create comparable learning while preserving judgement for case-specific conditions.
column19: The process should also test franchisee incentives, willingness and trust, DPE support capacity, and data quality. I would explicitly distinguish three situations: the diagnosis was wrong, the plan was appropriate but poorly executed, or the store economics are not recoverable. Otherwise the organisation may redesign the plan repeatedly when the real issue is implementation or viability.

column3: I think the hardest challenge would be balancing support for the franchisee with the need to step in when underperformance becomes serious. DPE would need to make sure there is clear responsibility for who is monitoring the store, who is working with the franchisee, and when the issue should be escalated. If those roles or decision points are unclear, different people could have different views on how serious the problem is or what action should be taken, which could delay the response.
column4: I would expect DPE to first confirm the extent and causes of the underperformance using store performance information and input from the franchisee. From there, the relevant Franchise Consultant or Market Manager would likely work with the franchisee to agree on a recovery plan, with clear actions, responsibilities and timeframes. The store?€?s progress would then be monitored against that plan, with additional support or escalation if performance did not improve. If the store continued to underperform despite reasonable recovery efforts, I would expect the case to be reviewed by more senior management to decide on the most appropriate formal outcome, such as a transfer, refranchising or closure.
column5: I?€?d focus on three areas: store performance trends like sales and profitability, operational issues such as staffing and service quality, and franchisee or management factors. Together, these should give DPE a clearer idea of what is actually driving the underperformance.

column15: I rated it a 5 because inconsistency at any stage could easily delay recovery or lead to the wrong actions being taken. If the problem is diagnosed differently, the plan is unclear, or follow-up is inconsistent, it would be much harder to get a sustained improvement across stores.
column16: Intervention process & control ?€? diagnosis, recovery planning, execution and follow-up
column17: I chose intervention process and control because even if DPE identifies the problem correctly, recovery can still fail if the plan, execution or follow-up is inconsistent. Governance and decision rights would probably be my second choice, especially if it is unclear who owns the case or when it should be escalated.
column18: I would introduce one clear and consistent recovery process for all seriously underperforming stores, with defined responsibilities, actions, timeframes and escalation points. That would make it easier to manage cases consistently and reduce the chance of issues being missed or dragging on.
column19: One thing I would also look at is whether franchisees are actually willing and able to follow the recovery plan. Even with a good process, limited engagement, capability or communication between DPE and the franchisee could still make recovery difficult.

column3: The hardest challenge is identifying the real cause of the underperformance early enough and making sure the right people take responsibility for fixing it. If diagnosis, accountability or communication are unclear, the recovery process can become slow and inconsistent.
column4: I would expect DPE to first review the store?€?s financial and operational performance, identify the main causes of underperformance, and discuss the findings with the franchisee and relevant support teams. A recovery plan should then be created with clear actions, responsibilities, targets and review dates. Progress should be monitored regularly. If the store does not improve, DPE should reassess the causes and consider stronger actions such as refranchising, transfer or closure.
column5: I would focus on store financial performance, operational performance such as sales, customer service and labour efficiency, and local market conditions including competition and customer demand. Franchisee capability and compliance with operating standards would also be important.

column8: If the initial diagnosis is inaccurate or incomplete, the recovery plan may focus on the wrong problems. This can lead to wasted effort, repeated changes and delays even if the later stages are managed properly.

column15: A recovery process depends on consistent diagnosis, planning, execution and review. If these stages are handled differently between cases, important causes may be missed, responsibilities may become unclear and decisions may be delayed. This makes sustainable recovery less likely and increases the chance of repeated corrective actions.
column16: Intervention process & control ?€? diagnosis, recovery planning, execution and follow-up
column17: The intervention process connects diagnosis, action and monitoring. If this process is inconsistent, even good performance information may not lead to effective action. Governance and decision rights would be a close second because clear escalation and accountability are also important.
column18: I would introduce a standardised recovery framework for all seriously underperforming stores. It should define how problems are diagnosed, who is responsible for each action, what success measures are used, and when escalation is required. This would improve consistency, accountability and decision making across cases.
column19: It may also be useful to ask how feedback from previous recovery cases is captured and shared across the franchise network. Lessons from successful and unsuccessful interventions could help DPE improve future recovery decisions.
